pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 9–11 (REPRESENTATIONAL). Reading a cladogram — the branching tree scientists use to show evolutionary relationships — taught by building and tracing trees from shared characters, so the tree becomes a tool the child reads, not decoration.
• Standards — UK (DfE): Y6 Evolution & inheritance (living things have changed over time; classification) and KS2 working-scientifically (identifying patterns, using evidence); leads to KS3 classification and evolution.
• Standards — US (NGSS): MS-LS4-2 (use anatomical similarities and differences to infer evolutionary relationships and construct explanations). Cladograms are the canonical representation for this idea.
• Operational details: teach that a shared derived character (e.g. feathers, three-toed foot) marks a branch point; two species are more closely related if they share a MORE RECENT common ancestor — traced by walking down the branches to where they meet, NOT by how close the tips sit on the page. Practise: read most-recent-common-ancestor, add a new species by its characters, and see the tree can be rotated at any node without changing relationships.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (concrete, ~9): point to where two animals' lines join — their most recent common ancestor. Tier B (transitional, ~10): decide which two of three species are most closely related using branch points (not tip proximity). Tier C (formal, ~11): place a new species on the tree using its shared characters, and explain why rotating a branch doesn't change relatedness.
bestPractices: Teach relatedness as 'most recent common ancestor', found by tracing branches down to a node — the single most important reading skill.
Directly confront the tip-proximity misconception with paired examples where the physically-nearest tip is NOT the closest relative.
Show node rotation early so children learn a tree encodes branching order, not left-right layout.
Ground each node in a shared derived character (a trait that appeared once and is inherited), linking anatomy to the tree.
Have children ADD a taxon by its characters, moving from reading to constructing, which cements how trees are built from evidence.
keyRepresentations: A cladogram with clearly marked internal nodes (common ancestors) and labelled character changes on branches.
A character matrix (rows=species, columns=traits) beside the tree it produces.
A 'trace two tips to their join' highlight showing the MRCA.
A rotate-the-node animation demonstrating relationships are preserved.
A trap layout: an adjacent tip that is actually a distant relative.
commonMisconceptions: 'Species closer together on the page are more closely related' — relatedness is set by shared ancestors (nodes), not tip distance.
'A cladogram is a ladder of progress toward more advanced forms' — it shows branching, not ranking; living tips are all equally 'modern'.
'The species at the far right/top is the most evolved' — orientation is arbitrary; nodes can rotate freely.
'Ancestors are the tips' — ancestors are the internal nodes, not the living species at the ends.
'Sharing any trait means close relationship' — only shared DERIVED characters define a clade; shared ancestral traits do not.

learn.summary: For ages 9–11, teach reading a cladogram (the branching tree showing evolutionary relationships) as an active tracing and building skill: find relatedness by tracing branches down to the most recent common ancestor (MRCA) node, not by how near two tips sit on the page. Learners place species by their shared derived characters, trace pairs to their joining node, test that rotating a branch leaves relationships unchanged, and confront the tip-proximity misconception directly.

activities.title: Build the tree from a character checklist
feedback: If the learner places a species by overall resemblance rather than a specific shared character, ask which single trait marks the branch they chose and whether the species actually has it.
When placement is correct, confirm the shared derived character that defines that branch (e.g. 'feathers appear at this node, so everything beyond it shares that ancestor').

Note that only shared DERIVED characters define a clade; a trait inherited from an older ancestor and also found in animals outside the group (an ancestral trait) does not pinpoint close relationship.
activities.rationale: Moving from reading to constructing cements how trees are built from evidence; having children add a taxon by its characters links anatomy to the tree structure. This construction pedagogy is a research-informed proposal, not directly validated by the cited sources, so no source claim is attached here.
learnerActions: Use a character matrix or checklist (feathers? teeth? three-toed foot?) and tick which traits a mystery animal has.

Place the animal onto the branch defined by the shared derived characters (newer traits) it has in common with others, so grouping follows those shared derived features, not overall physical resemblance or left-to-right order.
Add a new species to a partially completed cladogram using only its listed features, then explain which shared character justifies its position.
activities.intendedInsight: A cladogram is built from shared derived characters: in a simple classroom tree, a marked node shows where a new trait is assumed to have appeared in a common ancestor and been passed on to its descendants (some may later lose it), so species group by shared ancestry evidenced by shared derived features.

activities.title: Trace two tips to their most recent common ancestor
feedback: If the learner names an internal node's identity wrongly, remind them the node stands for a shared ancestor, not one of the species shown at the tips (which may be living or extinct).
If they pick the pair drawn side by side, have them trace both pairs to their joining nodes and compare which node is more recent.
Reinforce that a pair whose lines meet at a more recent node (closer to the tips) is more closely related than a pair whose lines meet only at the base.
activities.rationale: Tracing to the node makes the abstract 'relatedness' concept into a concrete, repeatable reading procedure grounded in the diagram's structure.
sourceClaims: A cladogram shows evolutionary relationships; two taxa are more closely related if they share a more recent common ancestor, read by tracing branches to the node where they join.
learnerActions: Pick two species (e.g. a shark and a lizard) and trace the lines down each branch until they meet at a node.
State that the meeting node is their most recent common ancestor and that this, not tip nearness, sets how closely related they are.
Given three species, decide which two are most closely related by comparing where each pair's branches join.
activities.intendedInsight: Relatedness is read as 'most recent common ancestor', found by tracing branches down to the node where two lines meet — a central tree-reading skill.

activities.title: The trap: nearest tip is not the closest relative
feedback: If the learner still chooses adjacent tips, trace each pair back to its branching node together and compare the depths of those nodes.
Confirm success when the learner cites the more recent shared node rather than side-by-side placement.

Address the related error that the top/far-right species is 'most advanced': each tip has its own mix of older and newer traits, and in dinosaur trees many tips are extinct species from different times, so a tip's position does not show it is more advanced.
activities.rationale: Directly confronting the tip-proximity misconception with paired examples where the nearest tip is not the closest relative targets the most common tree-reading error.
sourceClaims: Common tree-reading errors include equating tip proximity with relatedness and reading a 'ladder of progress'; relationships are unchanged by rotating branches at a node.
learnerActions: Examine a layout where two animals are drawn right next to each other but their traced lines only meet at the very base of the tree.
Find an animal drawn far across the page whose line meets one of them at a much more recent node.
Decide and explain which animals are actually most closely related, justifying the answer by the branching, not the page position.
activities.intendedInsight: Physical closeness of tips on the page does not indicate relatedness; only the recency of the shared ancestor (node) does.

activities.title: Rotate a branch and check what stays the same
feedback: If the learner thinks rotation changed relationships, have them re-trace the same pair to the same node before and after rotating.
Confirm understanding when they state that the order of tips is arbitrary and no tip is 'higher' or more evolved than another.
Reinforce that on a cladogram the ancestors are the internal nodes, not the tips; every tip, living or extinct, is drawn as a branch end, not as the ancestor of another tip.
activities.rationale: Showing node rotation early teaches that the diagram's meaning lives in its branching structure, not its drawn arrangement, pre-empting 'ladder of progress' and 'most evolved tip' errors.
sourceClaims: Common tree-reading errors include equating tip proximity with relatedness and reading a 'ladder of progress'; relationships are unchanged by rotating branches at a node.
learnerActions: Rotate a node so the tips swing to new left-right positions.
Re-trace two previously compared tips and confirm their meeting node — and so their relatedness — is unchanged.
Explain in their own words why rotating a branch, or the left-to-right order of tips, does not change which species are most closely related.
activities.intendedInsight: A tree encodes branching order (ancestry), not left-right layout; orientation is arbitrary and rotating at a node preserves all relationships.

constraints: A multiple-choice or click-the-node assessment (e.g. 'which two are most closely related?' with an adjacent-but-distant tip as the trap, or 'find the shared common ancestor') can probe and surface tip-proximity errors, but recognition-only responses do not require the learner to construct a tree or place a new taxon independently.

A single annotated cladogram with tappable nodes (tap to reveal 'feathers appear here', tap two tips to highlight their join) usefully introduces the parts, but a fixed single tree cannot let the learner test readings across different trees or experience that rotation preserves relationships; treat it as an introductory scaffold.

A spoken walkthrough from a scientist (e.g. 'how do you decide where a new fossil goes on the tree?') can convey reasoning, but reading a cladogram is a visual-procedural skill that benefits from hands-on tracing and placement; dialogue alone does not supply that practice.

Live, recomputing state (species snapping to the correct branch when characters are ticked; a trace tool lighting the path from two tips to their meeting node; a rotate control that visibly preserves relationships; a deliberate close-but-distant trap tip) can make the learning mechanism concrete; these are illustrative interaction options, not a required toolset — paper trees, card cutouts, and drawn-and-traced diagrams can serve the same purposes.
Use shared DERIVED characters, not any shared trait, to define clades; grouping by overall resemblance or by ancestral traits does not establish close relationship.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the listed sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The two cited sources are marked verified:false in the row; treat their claims as unverified references.

The original row asserted that a 3D rendering 'adds no spatial information' and that a static image 'can't' teach the core competence, and framed one medium as uniquely able to 'dismantle' the misconception. These comparative-necessity claims are not established by the cited sources; they have been softened to scoped affordances/limits in constraints rather than stated as universal laws.

The construction-from-characters activity (Build the tree from a character checklist) is a proposal; neither cited source directly evidences that building a tree from a character checklist is necessary or more effective than other methods, so its sourceClaims list is empty.

The error pattern 'a species evolved directly FROM the one next to it' references a prerequisite reteach (an internal ID in the source); the corrective move — internal nodes are the ancestors, tips are all endpoints — is preserved in activity feedback without that ID.

probeDeeper: If I rotated this branch so two species swapped sides, would that change which are most closely related? Why not?
What does a branching point (a node) on the diagram actually stand for?
Two species look almost identical but sit on far-apart branches — which matters more for relatedness, their looks or the branching?
assess.correctAnswer: The two most closely related species are the ones that share the most recent common ancestor — the nearest branching point — NOT necessarily the two drawn side by side. The new species is placed on the branch defined by the features it shares, grouping by shared derived features rather than by physical resemblance or left-to-right order.

errorPatterns.pattern: The two species drawn next to each other are the most related.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace each pair back to its branching node; relatedness is the recency of the common ancestor, not nearness along the row of tips.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks adjacent tips regardless of where the branches actually join.

errorPatterns.pattern: The species at the top or far end is the most 'advanced' or highest.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rotate a branch to show the order of tips is arbitrary — no tip is higher or more advanced than another.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Ranks the tips as more or less evolved by their position in the diagram.

errorPatterns.pattern: A species evolved directly FROM the one drawn next to it on the diagram.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point to the internal nodes as the shared ancestors; the tips are all endpoints, none is the ancestor of another.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names one living tip as the ancestor of another tip.

responseLevels.gap: Reads relatedness off the left-right nearness of the tips and/or ranks species as more or less advanced by position.
responseLevels.full: Identifies relatedness by most recent common ancestor, places a new species by its shared features, and explains that rotating branches and the order of tips don't change the relationships.
responseLevels.partial: Knows the diagram shows relationships and can read an explicitly marked shared node, but reverts to tip-proximity or resemblance when adding a new species.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Look at this cladogram of dinosaurs. First: point to the two species that are most closely related and tell me how the diagram shows that. Then: here is a new species with [list of shared features] — add it to the cladogram in the right place and explain why you put it there.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who reads tip-adjacency picks whichever two happen to be drawn next to each other. A child who reads the branching structure traces each pair back to its nearest shared node, and places a new species by its shared features.
